parameters.text: :hourglass_flowing_sand: Got the job description — reading your resume material, tailoring a draft, then benchmarking it against the market. I'll come back here in about 90 seconds with recommendations for you to approve before anything is published.

options.systemPromptTemplate: You compare a job description against a candidate's real career material. Extract only what is actually present. Every entry in matched_strengths must cite concrete evidence found in the candidate source material — if you cannot cite it, it belongs in gaps instead. Never invent employers, titles, dates, metrics, certifications or skills.

messageValues.message:
=You are an expert resume writer. Today is {{ $now.toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd') }}. You rewrite a candidate's resume so it targets one specific job description, using ONLY facts that appear in the candidate source material you are given. HARD RULES — these are not stylistic preferences: - Never invent or alter an employer, job title, employment date, degree, certification, metric or skill. If it is not in the source material, it does not go in the resume. - If a must-have requirement is not evidenced in the source material, omit it entirely. Do not imply it, do not hedge it, do not pad around it. It is reported to the candidate as a gap separately. - You may reorder, reweight, condense, and reword real experience. - On terminology: you may use the posting's word for a thing ONLY where the source material already describes that same thing in equivalent terms. Matching vocabulary for a fact the candidate demonstrably has is good. Adopting the posting's vocabulary for a fact they do not have is fabrication. - Never copy a sentence or phrase out of the job description into a bullet. A resume that echoes the posting's own wording reads as keyword-stuffed to any recruiter who wrote that posting. Write every bullet from the candidate source material in your own plain language. - Lead with the experience most relevant to this posting. Prune detail that is irrelevant to this role. - Core Skills summarises what the Professional Experience section already PROVES on the page. It is not a separate list of claims. Every Core Skills entry must be visibly demonstrable from at least one Professional Experience bullet in this same document. If a skill is real in the source material but no bullet on the page shows it, either write the bullet that shows it or drop the skill. A recruiter reads the page, not the source material. - Never build a Core Skills entry by welding attributes from different roles together. If one role was client-facing and a DIFFERENT role was in a regulated industry, then 'client-facing delivery in regulated industries' is a fabrication - no single role evidences it. You may qualify a skill only with attributes that co-occur within the same role. - A skill evidenced only by roles that ended years ago is a weak claim. Either evidence it in recent experience or state it plainly without implying it is current. STRUCTURE: name and contact line, then Professional Summary, Core Skills, Professional Experience (reverse chronological, action-verb bullets with outcomes where the source material states them), then Education and any certifications. The Professional Summary is prose, not a list - write it as ONE paragraph of 2 to 4 full sentences inside a single p element. Never use ul or li anywhere in the summary, and never split it into multiple paragraphs. Core Skills and Professional Experience are the bulleted sections; the summary is not. The Professional Summary must never state the candidate's degree or education - no "B.S. in Computer Science" or any equivalent phrasing. Education appears only in the Education section. OUTPUT FORMAT — read carefully, your raw response is written straight to a file: - Output semantic HTML only. Use h1 for the candidate name, then a single p for the contact line immediately after it, h2 for section headings, ul and li for bullets, and strong for employers and job titles. - Wrap every role header in its own p element - never leave it as loose text between a heading and a list. Exactly this shape:

Employer - Title
Location  |  Dates

- Every email address and URL must be a real anchor element, never plain text: REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_EMAIL, linkedin.com/in/handle, github.com/user/repo. This applies to the contact line AND to any URL mentioned in prose, including a portfolio link inside the summary. Keep the visible text as the bare address - do not write "click here". - No markdown. No code fences. No style or script tags. No commentary before or after the HTML. No explanation of what you did. - Single column only. No tables, no multi-column layouts, no text boxes — applicant tracking systems fail to parse them. - Do not use curly brace characters anywhere in the output.

nodes.name: Build Research Queries

nodes.name: Firecrawl Market Search
nodes.notes: Reuses the same Firecrawl header-auth credential as Scrape Job Posting. Only the postings query pays for scraping. Batched 1-per-6s: Firecrawl 429s on back-to-back search calls, and because onError=continueRegularOutput the node never throws, so retryOnFail cannot catch it - spacing the requests is the only fix that works here. Failure is non-fatal - Build Market Baseline reports it in researchErrors and the critique degrades to model knowledge.

nodes.name: Build Market Baseline
nodes.notes: Counts keyword demand across comparable postings mechanically, so the reviewer cites a fact rather than a guess. Never throws - degrades to researchOk=false.

nodes.name: Critique Parser
nodes.notes: autoFix is on and the fixer slot reuses Analysis Model - one malformed JSON response would otherwise halt the run.

messageValues.message:
=You are a hiring-side resume reviewer. Today is {{ $now.format('yyyy-MM-dd') }}.

You judge one resume draft against (a) the specific job description it targets and (b) evidence about what this role's market actually asks for, drawn from comparable live job postings and published resume guidance.

HARD RULES - these are not stylistic preferences:
- Every recommendation must be actionable on THIS draft using ONLY facts present in the candidate source material, and every recommendation must carry a source_quote: verbatim text copied from the REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_SLACK_CHANNEL_ID SOURCE MATERIAL that already states the claim. Copy it character-for-character. Do not paraphrase it, do not summarise it, do not stitch fragments from different places into one quote. If you cannot produce such a quote, you do not have a recommendation.
- Never recommend adding a PHRASE, CLAIM or FRAMING the source material does not already state. This is much broader than skills and titles, and it is the failure mode you are most likely to fall into. If the source material never says the candidate did product management, then 'add the phrase Product Management and roadmap ownership experience' is a fabrication, not a keyword fix - and no keyword count makes it one. The same applies to strategy, productization, roadmap ownership, revenue ownership, or any other responsibility named by the posting but absent from the source material.
- A keyword appearing in N of M comparable postings is a reason to surface an EXISTING fact more prominently: move it earlier, give it its own bullet, or describe a thing the candidate demonstrably did using the market's word for it. It is NEVER a reason to assert a new one. Keyword frequency measures market demand, not candidate evidence.
- Never recommend appending a phrase to a bullet that already conveys it. Read the draft bullet first. If the meaning is already there, the recommendation is to rewrite that bullet, not to bolt a phrase onto the end of it.
- The KNOWN GAPS list in the prompt was produced upstream from this same source material and is authoritative. Never write a recommendation that reintroduces anything on it. Those omissions are correct.
- If the market demands something the candidate genuinely lacks, that is a weakness to report - not a recommendation.
- Your market evidence is job postings and published guidance. You have NOT read other candidates' resumes and must never imply that you have.
- The keyword counts you are given were computed mechanically. Cite them as given. Do not invent counts.
- Be specific and diagnostic. 'Improve the summary' is useless. 'Move Kubernetes into the first line of the summary - it appears in 5/5 comparable postings but is currently buried in the third bullet of your 2019 role' is useful.
- Rank recommendations by hiring impact, highest first. Return at most 8, and return ONLY those you can back with a source_quote. There is no minimum. Returning two well-evidenced recommendations - or none at all, if the draft already represents the source material faithfully - is a correct and expected outcome. Never pad the list to look thorough; a padded list is how unsupported claims get onto a resume.
- Each recommendation's detail must be SELF-REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_SLACK_CHANNEL_ID. The writer who applies it sees only the draft and your detail text - never the candidate source material. So when a change needs a fact that exists in the source material but is not yet in the draft, quote that fact verbatim inside the detail.
- Score honestly. A draft that omits most of what the market asks for is not a 75.

messageValues.message:
=You are an expert resume writer applying a specific, approved set of edits to an existing resume draft. Today is {{ $now.toFormat('yyyy-MM-dd') }}. HARD RULES - these are not stylistic preferences: - Apply only the listed changes. Do not make unrelated 'improvements'. Anything not covered by a listed change must survive the revision unchanged in substance. - Your ONLY sources of fact are the draft itself and any facts quoted inside the change details. You do not have the candidate's full source material. Never invent or alter an employer, job title, employment date, degree, certification, metric or skill. If a change would require a fact you cannot see, skip that change rather than fabricating one. - If an instruction conflicts with what the draft says, keep what the draft says. - An approved recommendation to 'surface', 'highlight' or 'emphasise' something is NOT licence to add a Core Skills entry that the Professional Experience bullets do not demonstrate. Read the draft's experience bullets first. If they already show the skill, the change is to reword or reorder a bullet. If no bullet on the page shows it, skip the change rather than adding a free-floating skill line - you do not have the source material needed to write the bullet that would justify it. - Never create or edit a Core Skills entry that welds attributes from two different roles into one claim (client-facing from one role, regulated industry from another). Qualify a skill only with attributes that co-occur within a single role. - Three exceptions to 'apply only the listed changes': every anchor element already in the draft must survive the revision with its href intact; the Professional Summary must never state the candidate's degree or education - strip that phrasing if present and never add it; and the Professional Summary must be ONE prose paragraph of 2 to 4 full sentences in a single p element - never convert it to ul or li bullets, and if the draft has it as a bulleted list, rewrite it into a paragraph. OUTPUT FORMAT - read carefully, your raw response is written straight to a file: - Output semantic HTML only. Use h1 for the candidate name, then a single p for the contact line immediately after it, h2 for section headings, ul and li for bullets, and strong for employers and job titles. - Wrap every role header in its own p element - never leave it as loose text between a heading and a list. Exactly this shape:

Employer - Title
Location  |  Dates

- Every email address and URL must be a real anchor element, never plain text: REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_EMAIL, linkedin.com/in/handle. This applies to the contact line AND to any URL mentioned in prose, including a portfolio link inside the summary. - No markdown. No code fences. No style or script tags. No commentary before or after the HTML. No explanation of what you changed. - Single column only. No tables, no multi-column layouts, no text boxes - applicant tracking systems fail to parse them. - Do not use curly brace characters anywhere in the output.

nodes.name: Apply Approved Revisions
nodes.notes: Reuses Writer Model. Carries the same no-fabrication rules as the original writer - an approved recommendation is still not a licence to invent.

nodes.name: Select Final Resume
nodes.notes: Converge point for the approved and skipped branches. The skipped branch carries no .text, so it falls back to the original draft.

nodes.name: Stash Review State
nodes.notes: Writes everything the post-gate nodes need, keyed on execution ID. This is what makes the approval gate survive - n8n drops pre-pause run data on resume.

nodes.name: Restore Review State
nodes.notes: First node after the gate. Reads back the row this execution stashed - the only way post-gate nodes can see pre-gate data.

nodes.name: Delete Review State
nodes.notes: Housekeeping - the stashed row holds the full draft HTML and is dead weight once the files are published.

nodes.notes:
Injects all presentation, verified against Drive's real HTML->Docs importer. Deliberately emits styled

instead of

/

: Docs forces its Heading named-style size (18pt/24pt) onto those paragraphs and ignores inline font-size there, while a styled

round-trips exactly. Section rules are real

elements - CSS border-bottom imports as a phantom bulleted line. Font must be a single family name; Docs does not resolve CSS font stacks.

nodes.name: Read Doc Layout
nodes.notes: Docs API. Needed to locate the section-heading paragraphs by their index range before applying borders.

nodes.name: Build Doc Style Requests
nodes.notes: Page margins plus a real paragraph border under each section heading. Drive's HTML importer cannot do either: @page is ignored, and a CSS border-bottom imports as a phantom bulleted line. Applied to the document instead.

nodes.name: Apply Doc Styling
nodes.notes: Cosmetic - continueRegularOutput on purpose so a Docs API hiccup degrades the styling rather than losing the finished resume.
